claims.text: Enhanced free-energy integration coupled with machine-learned interatomic potentials can accurately predict melting temperatures across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach can accurately predict enthalpies of fusion across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach can accurately predict entropies of fusion across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach can accurately predict volume changes at melting across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach can accurately predict liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The coupled approach is computationally efficient across a broad HEA compositional space.
Enhanced sampling efficiently overcomes free-energy barriers near melting.
Enhanced sampling successfully captures solid-liquid phase-coexistence states during melting.
Accurate machine-learned interatomic potentials enable precise energetic calculations in HEAs.
Resolving the free-energy landscape and free-energy differences permits estimation of finite-temperature transition properties.
The resulting melting-temperature predictions will agree with high-precision experiments to approximately ±10 K.
Fusion enthalpy and entropy predictions will have accuracy comparable to the asserted ±10 K melting-temperature performance.
Predicted volume changes at melting will have accuracy comparable to the asserted ±10 K melting-temperature performance.
Traditional calorimetry often suffers from baseline issues or slow throughput.
Brute-force molecular dynamics has computational or sampling limitations in complex multicomponent systems.
Extreme compositional imbalances may cause the proposed approach to fail.
Inadequately trained machine-learned potentials may cause the proposed approach to fail.
Sampling efficiency may degrade under conditions far from the melting transition.
The quantitative error depends on interatomic-potential quality and enhanced-sampling efficiency.
The approach is falsified if more than 50% of tested HEAs deviate from experiment by over ±10 K in melting temperature or exceed acceptable error margins for latent heat or volume change.
